title: The Barbara Chain
question: All mammals are warm-blooded. All whales are mammals. Therefore, all whales are warm-blooded. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Barbara's chain links cleanly: whales sit inside mammals, mammals inside warm-blooded, so whales land inside warm-blooded. Valid form, true premises.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. All S are M plus all M are P guarantees all S are P — the terms nest like bowls. Validity here is structural; truth of premises makes it sound too.
lessonContent:
Nesting terms guarantee nesting conclusions.
All-S-are-M plus all-M-are-P always yields all-S-are-P.
Bowls-inside-bowls picture every Barbara.
Form validity plus true premises equals soundness.

title: The Backward Proof
question: If it rains, the streets get wet. The streets are wet. Therefore, it rained. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Wet streets have many causes — cleaners, burst pipes, sprinklers. Affirming the consequent mistakes one sufficient condition for the only one.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'If rain then wet' plus 'wet' never yields 'rain': consequences outnumber their causes. Affirming the consequent is the most committed fallacy in daily reasoning.
lessonContent:
Consequences outnumber their causes always.
Sufficient is not necessary — rain suffices, others too.
Backward proofs need ruling out rivals.
'If P then Q; Q' stops exactly there.

title: The Dry Denial
question: If the oven reaches full heat, the bread browns. The oven never heated. Therefore, the bread stayed pale. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Denying the antecedent forgets rival browners — broilers, blowtorches, yesterday's bake. No heat removes one cause, not all.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'If heat then brown' plus 'no heat' leaves every other browning method standing. Pale needs ruling out all causes, and the argument rules out one.
lessonContent:
Removing one cause removes only one cause.
Broilers and torches survive every oven denial.
Pale conclusions need all causes excluded.
Antecedents deny; consequents stay standing.

title: The Forward Step
question: If the alarm rings, classes empty. The alarm rings. Therefore, classes empty. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Modus ponens: the trigger fired, so the guaranteed result follows. Forward steps from true conditionals never misfire.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'If P then Q' plus 'P' delivers Q by the simplest valid move in logic. Ponens affirms forward; only backward moves (affirming Q) break.
lessonContent:
Triggers fired deliver guaranteed results.
Forward moves from true conditionals never misfire.
Ponens is logic's simplest valid step.
Affirm the antecedent; collect the consequent.

title: The Full Hallway
question: If the fuel ignites, the rocket lifts. The rocket sits on the pad. Therefore, the fuel never ignited. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Modus tollens: the guaranteed result absent means the trigger never fired. Grounded rockets testify against ignition.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'If ignition then liftoff' plus 'no liftoff' kills ignition — the result's absence testifies against its trigger. Pads hold rockets whose fuel slept.
lessonContent:
Grounded rockets testify against ignition.
Absent results eliminate their triggers.
Tollens takes away what ponens would give.
'No liftoff' is evidence about fuel, full stop.

title: The Shared Circle
question: All violins are instruments. All trumpets are instruments. Therefore, all violins are trumpets. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Sharing the orchestra never merges the sections. The middle term must connect extremes, not merely room with both.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Instruments' sits undistributed in both premises — it never speaks about all instruments, so violins and trumpets float unlinked inside it. Shared stages prove nothing about players.
lessonContent:
Shared stages never merge the sections.
Middle terms must connect, not cohabit.
Undistributed middles float conclusions loose.
Link extremes through the middle, never beside it.

title: The Empty Net
question: No stars are planets. All suns are stars. Therefore, no suns are planets. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Celarent excludes cleanly: suns sit inside stars, stars wholly outside planets, so suns land outside too. Negative universals chain like positives.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'No M are P' plus 'all S are M' fences S outside P without exception. Exclusion inherits downward exactly as inclusion does.
lessonContent:
Exclusion inherits downward like inclusion.
Fences around big groups pen all subgroups.
Negative universals chain as cleanly as positives.
Outside-outside reasoning needs no extra rule.

title: The Partial Net
question: All birds have feathers. Some pets are birds. Therefore, some pets have feathers. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Darii carries the universal down to the partial case: the pet-birds inherit feathers with their birdhood. Some-premises yield some-conclusions legitimately.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'All M are P' plus 'some S are M' places those S inside P — the some-quantifier survives the trip. Partial premises license partial conclusions, never wholes.
lessonContent:
Universals descend safely onto partial cases.
Some-premises license some-conclusions only.
Pet-birds inherit with their birdhood intact.
Never inflate 'some' conclusions into 'all'.

title: The Partial Fence
question: No fish breathe air. Some swimmers are fish. Therefore, some swimmers do not breathe air. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Ferio fences the partial case out: the swimmer-fish inherit airlessness with their fishhood. Negative universals govern some-cases too.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'No M are P' plus 'some S are M' excludes those S from P — the fence covers subgroups partially present. Exclusion reaches the some-quantifier intact.
lessonContent:
Fences cover partial subgroups too.
Negative universals govern some-cases fully.
Excluded middles exclude their members.
Some-not conclusions are perfectly respectable.

title: The Bank Switch
question: All banks hold money. River banks are banks. Therefore, river banks hold money. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. 'Bank' shifts meaning mid-argument — financial versus riverside — making four terms, not three. Equivocation smuggles a second middle term aboard.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. Valid syllogisms need exactly three terms used consistently; 'bank' plays two roles, so the middle never connects. Same spelling is not same meaning — check term identity.
lessonContent:
Same spelling is never same meaning guaranteed.
Three terms means three, used consistently.
Equivocation smuggles extra middles aboard.
Check identity before chaining words.

title: The Double Negative
question: No sailors are pilots. No captains are sailors. Therefore, no captains are pilots. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Two negative premises never yield a conclusion — they exclude without connecting. Negatives fence apart; they cannot bridge.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'No A are B' plus 'no C are B' leaves A and C unlinked: both outside B, relation between them unknown. Exclusion without connection concludes nothing.
lessonContent:
Two negatives conclude nothing, ever.
Fences apart never bridge together.
Exclusion needs one inclusion to conclude.
Count the negatives before trusting chains.

title: The Horned Proof
question: All unicorns have exactly one horn. Therefore, some existing creature has exactly one horn. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Universal claims about unicorns say nothing about existence — 'all' can hold vacuously over an empty set. Existence is never a free conclusion.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'All unicorns' quantifies over zero actual beasts; universals hold vacuously without members. Modern logic demands existential import be earned, never assumed.
lessonContent:
Universals hold vacuously over empty sets.
Existence is never a free conclusion.
'All' describes members; it never creates them.
Earn existential import separately.

title: The Flipped All
question: All squares are rectangles. Therefore, all rectangles are squares. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Conversion fails for A-propositions: inclusion runs one way. Squares nest inside rectangles; rectangles sprawl far beyond squares.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'All A are B' never converts to 'all B are A' — nesting is directional. Long rectangles refute the flip instantly.
lessonContent:
Inclusion runs one direction only.
Nesting never reverses by conversion.
A-propositions convert illicitly, always.
Check direction before flipping quantifiers.

title: The Flipped None
question: No goalkeepers are strikers. Therefore, no strikers are goalkeepers. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. E-propositions convert cleanly: mutual exclusion is symmetric. No-overlap reads identically both directions.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'No A are B' and 'no B are A' say one symmetric thing: the positions never overlap. Exclusion, unlike inclusion, reverses safely.
lessonContent:
Exclusion is symmetric; inclusion is not.
No-overlap reads identically both ways.
E-propositions convert freely, always.
Symmetry belongs to fences, never nests.

title: The Flipped Some
question: Some students are athletes. Therefore, some athletes are students. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. I-propositions convert: overlap is symmetric. The shared members witness both directions at once.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'Some A are B' names overlapping members who are simultaneously B-that-are-A. Overlap, like exclusion, reverses without loss.
lessonContent:
Overlap reverses without any loss.
Shared members witness both directions.
I-propositions convert as freely as E ones.
Symmetry covers fences and overlaps alike.

title: The Long Chain
question: All A are B. All B are C. All C are D. Therefore, all A are D. This extended chain is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Sorites chains link Barbara repeatedly: nesting is transitive across any length. Bowls within bowls within bowls.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Each link is a valid Barbara, and validity composes: A⊆B⊆C⊆D yields A⊆D directly. Chains hold however long the nesting runs.
lessonContent:
Validity composes across any chain length.
Nesting is transitive without exception.
Each link checked makes the chain trustworthy.
Long sorites are repeated Barbaras.

title: The Mortal Socrates
question: All men are mortal. Socrates is a man. Therefore, Socrates is mortal. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. The textbook Barbara: Socrates sits inside men, men inside mortals, so Socrates lands inside mortals. Two millennia of agreement.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Singular premises ('Socrates is a man') function as universals about one member. Nest the individual, inherit the predicate — philosophy's most famous valid move.
lessonContent:
Individuals nest like classes with one member.
Singular premises behave universally.
Inherit predicates through membership.
Famous forms earned fame by never failing.

title: The Mortal Confusion
question: All soufflés are egg dishes. This omelette is an egg dish. Therefore, this omelette is a soufflé. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Egg dishes include frittatas, quiches, and omelettes — the omelette's membership proves nothing about souffléhood. Affirming the predicate proves nothing about the subject.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'All soufflés are egg dishes' plus 'omelette is an egg dish' is affirming the consequent in whites: egghood has countless sources. Shared predicates never identify subjects.
lessonContent:
Shared predicates never identify subjects.
Egghood has countless non-soufflé sources.
Consequent affirmed proves nothing backward.
Aprons don't rescue bad forms.

title: The Dry Streets
question: If frost comes, the basil dies. The basil thrives. Therefore, no frost came. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Thriving basil denies the guaranteed result, so the trigger never fired — textbook tollens. Absence of wilt testifies against frost.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'If frost then death' plus 'thriving' eliminates frost: results absent mean triggers absent. Denying the consequent is the safe backward move.
lessonContent:
Thriving testifies against frost directly.
Absent results eliminate their triggers.
Consequent denied denies antecedents safely.
Backward-safe moves mirror forward ones.

title: The Either Or
question: The alarm means fire or drill. It is not a drill. Therefore, it is a fire. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Disjunctive syllogism: eliminating one alternative leaves the other standing. Either-or plus not-one yields the other.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'P or Q' plus 'not P' delivers Q — elimination is deduction. Alternatives exhausted leave survivors standing.
lessonContent:
Elimination is deduction in disguise.
Exhausted alternatives leave survivors.
Either-or plus not-one yields the other.
Disjoin, deny, collect the remainder.

title: The Inclusive Trap
question: The pass covers bus or tram (or both). She rode the bus. Therefore, she did not ride the tram. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: False. Inclusive 'or' tolerates both — bus-plus-tram days exist. Affirming one alternative never denies the other.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — it is false. 'Or' in logic includes 'both' unless stated otherwise; affirming the bus leaves the tram entirely open. Both-together commutes break every exclusive reading.
lessonContent:
Logical 'or' includes 'both' by default.
Affirming one alternative denies nothing.
Both-together commutes break exclusive readings.
Check inclusivity before eliminating.

title: The If Chain
question: If you study, you pass. If you pass, you graduate. Therefore, if you study, you graduate. This chain is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Hypothetical syllogism links conditionals transitively: study routes through passing to graduating. If-chains compose like nesting.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. P→Q plus Q→R yields P→R — the middle consequent-antecedent cancels like middle terms. Conditional chains hold across any length.
lessonContent:
Conditionals compose transitively, always.
Middle links cancel like middle terms.
If-chains are Barbaras in disguise.
Link study to graduation stepwise.

title: The Pet Exclusion
question: No sharks are whales. Some hunters are sharks. Therefore, some hunters are not whales. This argument is valid.
correctExplanation: True. Ferio again in fins: the hunter-sharks inherit non-whaleness with their sharkhood. Partial premises, partial exclusions, full validity.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. 'No S are W' plus 'some H are S' fences those hunters outside whaleness. The some-quantifier carries exclusion faithfully to its members.
lessonContent:
Hunter-sharks inherit non-whaleness automatically.
Partial premises carry full exclusions.
Ferio wears fins without losing form.
Some-not conclusions close real arguments.

title: The Reverse Rule
question: A valid argument can have false premises and a false conclusion at the same time.
correctExplanation: True. Validity is form only: 'All fish fly; Nemo is a fish; so Nemo flies' is perfectly valid with every claim false. Form and truth travel separately.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Validity checks structure, never content — false premises can validly entail false conclusions. Soundness adds truth; validity alone promises only conditional safety.
lessonContent:
Form and truth travel separately always.
False premises can validly entail falsehoods.
Validity promises conditional safety only.
Soundness is validity plus truth.

title: The True Guarantee
question: A valid argument with true premises must always have a true conclusion.
correctExplanation: True. That guarantee defines deductive validity: true premises cannot validly lead astray. Soundness seals truth from assumptions to conclusion.
incorrectExplanation: It is true. Validity means impossibility of true-premises-plus-false-conclusion — that is the entire definition. Trust the seal: sound arguments never betray.
lessonContent:
Impossibility of true-to-false defines validity.
Seals hold from assumptions to conclusions.
Sound arguments never betray their premises.
Trust the guarantee; check the premises.
